title: Tyre, the Rock in the Sea, Will Fall
summary: Tyre, the great Phoenician trading city, rejoices that Jerusalem, a rival gateway of commerce, has been broken. God announces that he will bring many nations against Tyre like waves of the sea, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, and will scrape her down to a bare rock where fishermen spread their nets. The rulers of the coastlands lament her fall, and she is sent down to the Pit with the peoples of the ancient past.
story: Chapters 26 to 28 form the longest oracle in the book's collection against the nations, directed at Tyre and its sister city Sidon. Tyre receives three chapters, as much space as the four nations of chapter 25 combined, and only Egypt (chapters 29 to 32) receives more. The reason is Tyre's wealth and pride. Where the neighbors of chapter 25 gloated from spite, Tyre gloats from calculation: Jerusalem's fall means more trade for Tyre. Chapter 26 announces the judgment in straightforward terms; chapter 27 turns it into a lament over a sinking ship; chapter 28 addresses the city's king. Together they show a world economy built on pride, and God's claim to rule over it.
historical:
Tyre was the leading city of Phoenicia, on the coast of what is now southern Lebanon. Its main city stood on a rocky island a short distance offshore, with dependent settlements on the mainland (the daughters or villages of verses 6 and 8). The island's position made it almost impregnable to land armies, and its fleets and colonies, including Carthage in North Africa, gave it trade links across the Mediterranean. Hiram of Tyre had supplied David and Solomon with cedar and craftsmen (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Kings 5:1-12).

The date in verse 1 is uncertain, because the Hebrew text gives the year but does not name the month; translations reconstruct it differently. Either way the oracle belongs to the time of Jerusalem's fall in 587 or 586 BC. According to the Jewish historian Josephus, who cites Phoenician records, Nebuchadnezzar then besieged Tyre for thirteen years, probably from about 586 to 573 BC. The siege ended with Tyre submitting to Babylon, not with the city destroyed, and Ezekiel himself later acknowledges that Nebuchadnezzar's army gained little from it (29:17-20). In 332 BC Alexander the Great took the island city after a siege of about seven months by building a causeway from the mainland, using rubble from the old mainland settlement.
cultural:
Tyre's taunt in verse 2 is commercial. Jerusalem is called the gate to the nations, probably because Judah sat astride inland trade routes between Arabia, Egypt, and the north. With Jerusalem gone, Tyre expected to capture its share of the traffic. The prophets often judged the powerful not only for violence but for greed, and here Tyre's sin is to see a neighbor's catastrophe as a business opportunity.

The siege described in verses 7 to 12 is the standard siege of a land city, with ramps, battering rams, and cavalry in the streets. The Pit (verse 20) is a common Old Testament name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a place beneath the earth where the dead of all the ancient peoples lie. The lament of the princes of the sea (verses 16 to 18) uses real mourning customs: stepping down from thrones, removing robes, sitting on the ground. The coastlands were the islands and coastal peoples of the Mediterranean who traded with Tyre and depended on it.
literary: The chapter has four oracles, each beginning with this is what the Lord GOD says (verses 3, 7, 15, and 19). The first announces the judgment in general terms: many nations, like waves. The second names the agent, Nebuchadnezzar, and describes the siege in vivid detail. The third shifts to the reaction of the coastal princes and includes a short lament in the limping rhythm of a funeral song. The fourth sends Tyre down to the Pit. A pun runs through the chapter: the Hebrew name of Tyre, Tsor, means rock, and God promises to make the rock-city a bare rock (verses 4 and 14). The waves image of verse 3 is fitting for an island city and anticipates the shipwreck of chapter 27.

outline.t: Many nations like waves: Tyre made a bare rock
Nebuchadnezzar's siege and the city's ruin
The princes of the coastlands lament
Tyre sent down to the Pit

doctrines.note: God raises up Nebuchadnezzar and many nations against Tyre. The movements of empires and the fortunes of trading cities are under his rule, even when the actors do not know him.
Tyre is judged for treating Jerusalem's ruin as an opportunity for profit. The chapter shows God weighing economic pride and greed, not only violence.
Tyre's gloating reveals a heart that values others only by what can be gained from them. Pride, security in wealth, and indifference to suffering are presented as sins of a whole city.

words.note: Tsor, Tyre, a name meaning rock, after the rocky island on which the city stood. The chapter turns the name into a sentence: the rock will become a bare rock, scraped clean.
Sela, a crag or cliff. Combined with the word for bare, it describes what will remain of Tyre (verses 4 and 14): a sun-scorched rock where fishermen dry their nets.
I, coastland or island, used for the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean world. The coastlands tremble at Tyre's fall because their own trade depended on it.
Yarad, to go down. It describes the princes descending from their thrones in mourning (verse 16) and Tyre going down to the Pit (verse 20). The proud city that sat high is brought low.

christ: The New Testament takes up the language of Ezekiel's oracles against Tyre in Revelation 18, where the fall of Babylon the great is lamented by kings, merchants, and sailors who grew rich from her trade, using images drawn from this chapter and the next (compare the silenced music of Revelation 18:22 with verse 13). Babylon in Revelation stands for a world system built on pride, wealth, and oppression, and its fall makes way for the city of God. Jesus himself mentions Tyre and Sidon, saying that they would have repented long ago had they seen the mighty works done in Galilee (Matthew 11:21-22), and Mark records that people from the region of Tyre and Sidon came to him (Mark 3:8). These are uses of Tyre as a type of proud commercial power and of the nations' place in God's purposes, not predictions contained in this chapter.

hard.q: Nebuchadnezzar did not destroy Tyre, and a city called Tyre still exists. Did this prophecy fail?
hard.a: The difficulty is real and old. Nebuchadnezzar's thirteen-year siege ended with Tyre's submission, not its destruction, and Tyre was later rebuilt and remains a city today. Readers respond in several ways. Many point to verse 3, which speaks of many nations coming against Tyre like successive waves, and verse 12, which switches from he to they; on this reading the prophecy describes a process that included Nebuchadnezzar but was completed by later conquerors, notably Alexander the Great, who in 332 BC threw the rubble of the mainland city into the sea to build his causeway. Some add that the ancient island city lies largely in ruins beneath the later town. Others read the language as the stylized imagery of prophetic judgment oracles, which announce the end of a proud power in total terms; Tyre as an independent sea power did come to an end. A third observation is that the book itself preserves the tension. In 29:17-20, dated about sixteen years later, Ezekiel acknowledges that Nebuchadnezzar gained no wages from Tyre and promises him Egypt instead. Many readers find it significant that the book did not rewrite the earlier oracle, and they see here a picture of prophecy as God's word spoken into history, whose fulfillment can take shapes the prophet did not fully foresee.

questions: Tyre saw Jerusalem's ruin as a chance to profit. Where does our economic life encourage us to see others' misfortune as opportunity?
The coastlands trembled because their prosperity depended on Tyre. What would it mean for our security to rest in something that cannot fall?
How do you respond when a biblical prophecy seems not to have been fulfilled in the way you expected?
